messages.subject: truncation parameter
parts:
Hi all,

I have asked this question before, but with a complicated model so it was hard to see the actual problem. I have done a bit more work on it and realised that the same problem occurs in much simpler models, so I'm hoping someone can help me :)

Let say I produce a set of samples by the following code (I'm using pystan, but this shouldn't matter...):

### Parameters
xmin = 5     # Truncation location of data
mu = 4       # Mean of data
scale = 2.0  # Standard deviation of data

### Produce samples (final size ~5000)
xint = np.random.normal(loc=mu,scale=scale,size=15000)
xint = xint[xint>xmin]

### Add some measurement uncertainty
n = 2 + np.random.poisson(10**((xint-mu-0.5)))
sd = 2*np.clip(1 - 0.43*np.log10(n), 0.02, np.inf)
xobs = xint + np.random.normal(scale=_sd)

The addition of the uncertainty is a bit strange but corresponds in some rough way to how I add uncertainty to my real problem, where each variate represents a (dark matter) halo mass, and the halo mass is correlated with the number of galaxies within it, and the number of galaxies yields the measurement uncertainty. Basically you can think of it as adding large uncertainty to low-valued variates, and much less to high-valued variates. In any case, the final distribution looks like



Of course, there is some probability mass outside the shown range for the uncertain case (stuff that got scattered down). Also, the reason for the turnover in the intrinsic curve is just because it's a KDE. It really peaks at 5 or very close to it.

Anyway, to me the obvious way to code the Stan for parameter estimation is:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
    vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
    vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0,upper=10> xmin;
    vector<lower=xmin,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
}

model {
    xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
    for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
}

The interesting part is that xtrue has a  lower bound which is a parameter. When I run this through Stan (I ran 700 warmup and 2000 iterations for 4 chains), the first thing I notice is that it has a hard time converging -- each chain seems to settle in a different spot. But none of these spots are very close to the solution. In fact, they are all biased to high mu and low sigma. The median values for all chains are:

{u'lp__': -3491.0188530263313,
 u'mu': 6.33030908325631,
 u'sigma': 1.1798037697816155,
 u'xmin': 4.9482856755250273,
 u'xtrue': 6.5643129692386513}

The thing is, the iteration with highest likelihood has much higher likelihood than the "true" answer does. If "gaussmode" is the highest-likelihood iteration, then

print gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars({'mu':mu,"sigma":scale,"xmin":xmin,"xtrue":xint})) - gauss_fit.log_prob(gauss_fit.unconstrain_pars(gaussmode))

gives  -2518.74677702.

However, another way to formulate the model might be the following:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
    vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
    vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    vector<lower=0,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
}

transformed parameters {
    real xmin;
    xmin <- min(xtrue);
}

model {
    xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
    for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
}

This time, xtrue is left free, and xmin is chosen as the minimum of xtrue. This means that there is not a heavy jacobian adjustment on xtrue (since in the previous model, most of xtrue should be close to xmin, the jacobian adjustment becomes large and negative). Using this model, and doing exactly the same calculation as above (i.e. the log_prob at the truth minus the log_prob at the mode of the other model) gives a positive number, i.e. the truth is more likely.

Of course, just because it is more likely doesn't mean that that is where the probability density is. So, I then ran the same length chains with the "no mmin" model. This model ran a lot slower than the first (not sure why?). Again, each chain settles in a different place, so I guess I'd have to run longer to get convergence (or maybe it will never converge?), but here is the Stan summary:

Inference for Stan model: anon_model_2d2e212313b2a3b52815285bebd934ce.
4 chains, each with iter=2000; warmup=700; thin=1; 
post-warmup draws per chain=1300, total post-warmup draws=5200.

              mean se_mean     sd   2.5%    25%    50%    75%  97.5%  n_eff   Rhat
mu            5.79    0.18    0.4    4.8   5.54   5.88   6.09   6.31    5.0   2.38
sigma         1.44    0.09   0.17    1.2   1.32   1.41   1.57   1.86    4.0   2.52
xmin          4.81    0.04   0.08   4.67   4.74   4.82   4.88   4.92    4.0    2.5
lp__        3167.5   57.93 129.53 2935.1 3058.7 3181.9 3255.7 3414.5    5.0   2.07

This is a little closer to the truth than the first model in all but xmin. Still not very good though. The thing is, the mean likelihood is higher than the likelihood at the truth.

The last thing to see is the density plot of xtrue for each model. To plot, I just chose the highest likelihood iteration, but I don't think this choice affects the qualitative judgment of the outcome:



It seems like the second model does "better". I was wondering if there is any reason it *should* do better, or in fact if it should be different at all from the first model?

Cheers,
Steven

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] truncation parameter
parts:
Firstly, looking at point estimates is rarely if never helpful.
Bayes is about uncertainty, which means when you judge
a model you want to look at _intervals_, not points. The
question is wether, say, the 5-95% credible interval captures
the true value.

Secondly, neither of your models are correct. Please read
the section of the manual on truncation and censoring. To
build these models correctly you have think _generatively_
and match how you simulated the data. The latent x is
generated from a truanted normal, and then the measured
x is generated from the latent x. Also, don’t use bounds
and uniform priors.

data {
int<lower=0> N; // Number of samples
vector[N] x_meas; // Measured values
vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {

real mu;
real<lower=0> sigma;
real xmin;
vector<lower=xmin>[N] xtrue;
}

model {
mu ~ normal(0, 10);
sigma ~ cauchy(0, 5);
xmin ~ normal(0, 10);

// First model the latent x

// Then model the observation, note the swap
x_meas ~ normal(xtrue, uncertainty);

}

By thinking generatively you’ll also find that you want to model
the observation variability and not assume that you know it
absolutely. Even for a population based model like you mention
you have to consider that those populations are themselves
measured with uncertainty.

Thanks Michael for your reply,Sorry I didn't see it earlier -- I thought email notifications were on, but apparently not.

Firstly, sorry about the plots that were point estimates, I just didn't have plots at the time that were better representatives of the uncertainty distributions (I do now).

I have a few questions in reply. Firstly, I at least think I understand what you say about generative models. That was my approach to it. I guess switching xtrue and x_meas would have been more explicit in terms of the generative model approach, but I figured it didn't matter anyhow since the normal distribution is symmetric. Just in case this really was the thing that was driving the solution in the wrong direction, I've re-run swapping these two. The solutions are unchanged as far as I can tell, which is what I would expect.

I know using uniform priors with bounds is discouraged, but I thought it would be a reasonable place to start, and surely it shouldn't screw things up too much? I'll re-run again with the priors you suggest to make sure, but I wouldn't think putting extra weight on the wrong solution will fix the problem.

Just to be clear, the model I ran this time was:

data {
    int<lower=0> N;     // Number of samples
    vector[N] x_meas;   // Measured values
    vector<lower=0>[N] uncertainty; // Uncertainty in values
}

parameters {
    real<lower=0,upper=8> mu;
    real<lower=0> sigma;
    real<lower=0,upper=10> xmin;
    vector<lower=xmin,upper=30>[N] xtrue;
}

model {
    xtrue ~ normal(x_meas,uncertainty);
    for (i in 1:N) xtrue[i] ~ normal(mu,sigma)T[xmin,];
}

So here are some indicative results from my run:


Here the dark red region indicates the results from every iteration after warmup, and the bright red is the inner 68% region. Clearly, the upper end of the distribution is not pulled back to where it should be. This is the same behaviour I was seeing before, just now its a bit more robust. I ran several realisations, using different random seeds each time to produce the sample, and plot the marginalised posteriors of the parameters:



As you can see, all random samples lead to biased results in the same direction for mu and sigma. 


Oddly, this only occurs when the uncertainty is a function of the independent variable. If I produce my samples in exactly the same way, but then add a random gaussian number to each of them to bring them up to the same uncertainty (the maximum in the sample), then the bias disappears (though the resulting uncertainties on parameters are a bit larger). Any ideas on why this would be?


Thanks heaps for your help once again,


Steven
